# Follow the Sun

`customer_support.model.follow_the_sun` · model · parent `—`

> Continuous coverage bought by handing the open queue between two or three regional hubs at shift boundaries. Nobody works nights, and the customer is never told to wait until morning. That is the whole benefit, and it is a real one. . The cost is continuity, and it is paid at every boundary. An unresolved ticket crosses a hub edge once per shift; a ticket open for three days has been owned by nine people. Context that a single-region team keeps in an agent's head has to be written down here or it does not survive the night — which means the ticket record stops being documentation and becomes the operating mechanism. A handoff note that would be a nicety elsewhere is load-bearing here, and the failure is not that notes are bad but that they are optional. . The customer experiences the failure specifically: someone new asks them the same question every morning. That is what drives detractor scores in this model, far more than resolution time, and it is invisible in any metric the queue produces. . What an operator carries over wrongly from a single-region team: treating the assignee as the owner. In this branch the queue owns the ticket and the assignee holds a lease that expires at shift end. A ticket left assigned to a person who is asleep is the standard way a follow-the-sun queue stalls for eight hours while looking perfectly healthy on a dashboard. The second carry-over error is leaving the SLA clock configured to pause outside business hours — there are no business hours here, so a promise that used to consume one working day now consumes three calendar shifts, and the exposure triples silently.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | global user base; the same account raises tickets into whichever hub is awake |
| typical_resolution_hours | 20 |
| volume_shape | continuous with regional peaks; each hub inherits the previous hub's residue |
| staffing_model | two or three regional hubs with overlapping handoff windows |
| coverage | 24x7 by shift succession, no on-call — the point is that nobody is woken up |
| automation_level | moderate; deflection matters most in the thin hours of each hub |
| primary_channels | `ticket_portal`, `email`, `chat`, `phone` |
| notes | The handoff window is the incident risk. A major incident declared twenty minutes before a shift change gets two half-owners and no continuous narrative, and the customer-facing updates go quiet at exactly the moment they are most read. Incident command has to be held explicitly across the boundary rather than inherited with the queue.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `queue`, `status`, `assignee`


> Queue is the owner, assignee is a lease. Both are mandatory and they mean different things — a ticket with an assignee and no queue cannot be picked up by the next hub, and that is the most common stall in this model.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `due_at`, `action`


> "This afternoon" is not a commitment across three hubs; it is three different afternoons. Every promise has to resolve to an absolute instant, and the hub that will be awake at that instant is usually not the hub that made it.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `clock_state`


> Clocks run continuously here because coverage is continuous. That reads as generous and is the branch's largest hidden liability — the overnight hub is usually the thinnest, so exposure is highest exactly where capacity is lowest.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`


> Language and timezone belong on the requester, not inferred from whichever agent replied last. Inferring them is how a customer gets answered in three languages.
